name: Oxblood
lede: Oxblood is a very dark, slightly brownish red, named for the color of ox blood.

sections.title: A dark red named for blood
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines oxblood plainly as a dark red [1]. St Clair's list of color terms is more particular, calling it a dark rust-red [2]. Both are broad descriptions, and neither gives a date or a dyestuff, so the name is best treated as a plain comparison to the animal's blood rather than a pigment with a recorded history.

The swatch here is a much deeper, nearly black red than most people picture, which is common for names of this kind: the word covers a range, and the swatch is one pick from it [3].

sections.title: The porcelain glaze
sections.body: The French name *sang-de-boeuf* is literally "oxblood", and Paterson's dictionary uses it for a deep red glaze on old Chinese porcelain [4]. Separately, our name records show the English word oxblood first recorded in 1705, as Maerz and Paul's dictionary dates it; that source does not say the word was first used for the glaze [3]. The glaze is a ceramic effect, so its color depends on the clay, the firing and the light, and no single swatch can stand for it.

sections.title: Red as drama
sections.body:
According to St Clair, painters have long used reds from oxblood up to persimmon for drama and eroticism [2]. In our archive, a dark red close to this swatch turns up in 378 paintings, as photographed [3]. It is most often a shadow tone, which is what you would expect of a color this dark: in 43% of the 123 paintings where it covers enough canvas, it sits among the darkest values [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, at 2.5 times the museums' baseline rate [3]. Dark reds of this kind appear on canvas centuries before the word is recorded, so the match is a look-alike in aged photographs, not proof of a particular pigment [3].

Words like [[maroon]], [[burgundy]] and [[mahogany]] cover similar ground, as does [[wine-red]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our 23,781-painting archive the color appears in 378 paintings, more common than 62% of the named colors [3]. It keeps company with very dark browns and blacks, which fits its role as a shadow [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so the colors are as photographed.

origin.first_recorded: English color word; first recorded 1705 in our name records

questions.q: What does the French name sang-de-boeuf mean?
In which kind of old object does Paterson place the oxblood-red glaze?

openers: Oxblood is also a pottery color: the French name for it, sang-de-boeuf, is the old porcelain glaze.

issues: 1705 is the first record of the word oxblood, not a glaze date; rewrote the claim and the aside
